title: Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations
text: arXiv:2611.08269 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE cs.AI Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations Authors: Xiaobo Chen , Genliang Zhu , Ziyuan Wang , Chu Wang Abstract : After a runtime or API migration, an LLM- repaired procedure can run cleanly yet return wrong results, and a release check on typical test inputs ships it. We report a preregistered study of 73 tasks covering 60 documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite. Every candidate is executed on the real runtimes against withheld contracts. Over the complete… ▽ More After a runtime or API migration, an LLM- repaired procedure can run cleanly yet return wrong results, and a release check on typical test inputs ships it. We report a preregistered study of 73 tasks covering 60 documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite. Every candidate is executed on the real runtimes against withheld contracts. Over the complete repair space, the all-assertions gate on typical inputs released 0.410 of wrong repairs . One edge input written from the release note cut this to 0.065, and to 0.061 on 15 unseen clusters. Three inputs from a blind GPT-5.6-luna writer that never saw the program reached 0.070. Two further frozen stages enlarged the menu to 1491 fragments and then added 233 hard distractors that match the legacy output on typical inputs. The edge input (0.058) and the frontier-model writer (0.058) passed their preregistered tests. Yet 0.168 and 0.153 of the hard wrong programs still passed. Two local-model writers failed their preregistered tests. Across four model families, the edge input cut wrong releases per attempt in all three open-weight families on all three menus, for example from 0.233 to 0.057, without lowering correct completion. Self-tests helped less. A blind AI audit flagged 34 contracts as stricter than their requirements. Dropping the disputed checks changed 0 verdicts, but class-label disputes remain open. No model-written code was executed. Artifacts are available from the authors on request. △ Less Submitted 5 November, 2026; originally announced November 2026. Comments: 30 pages, 2 figures. Preregistered; artifacts are available from the authors on request ACM Class: D.2.5; D.2.7; I.2.2

title: How Should Agents See Code? Rethinking Code Representations for Agentic Software Engineering
text:
arXiv:2611.07286 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE cs.AI How Should Agents See Code? Rethinking Code Representations for Agentic Software Engineering Authors: Melika Sepidband , Jiho Shin , Song Wang , Hadi Hemmati Abstract : …We evaluate Claude Code with Haiku 4.5 against a raw-tool baseline on four repository-level tasks: fault localization with LinuxFLBench, repository-level code generation and repair with SWE-bench Pro, test generation with SWT-bench, and security patching with SecBench.
  The results show that representation workflows are most useful as token-saving tools wh… ▽ More LLM agents are increasingly used for repository-level software engineering tasks. However, most agents still access repositories through raw files, lexical search, and shell commands, treating code primarily as text. This paper investigates map-based code-representation workflows as a design variable in agentic software engineering, examining how different repository views change agents' retrieval behavior, task success, token use, and latency.
  In this paper, we study five code-representation workflows: abstract syntax trees, call graphs, module dependencies, documentation-enriched search, and a hybrid workflow that combines them. Each workflow exposes a repository map that the agent can query during a task. We evaluate Claude Code with Haiku 4.5 against a raw-tool baseline on four repository-level tasks: fault localization with LinuxFLBench, repository-level code generation and repair with SWE-bench Pro, test generation with SWT-bench, and security patching with SecBench.
  The results show that representation workflows are most useful as token-saving tools when localization is the bottleneck, while their success gains narrow when the decisive step is patch or test authoring . On LinuxFLBench, all five workflows improve recall@10 over the baseline (0.757-0.829 vs. 0.717) and reduce token usage by 25-39%. On SWE-bench Pro, resolution remains close to the baseline (44.3-50.6% vs. 49.0%) while token usage drops by 17-26%. On SecBench, Callgraph has the highest patch-resolution rate in this sample (34.3% vs. 28.9%) and uses fewer tokens, but all workflows increase latency. On SWT-bench, Hybrid and Docs have the highest reproducing-test rates in this sample (47.8% and 47.2% vs. 44.7%), but all workflows use more tokens and take longer. Overall, map-based workflows change both what the agent inspects and how much it spends, but their benefits are task-dependent rather than universal. △ Less Submitted 4 November, 2026; originally announced November 2026.

title: Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions
text: arXiv:2611.05390 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.MA Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions Authors: Fuad Ali Abstract : Multi-agent language-model systems often add a reviewer to improve an upstream agent's decision. Yet a reviewer can both repair errors and replace decisions that were already correct. We study this as a problem of institutional jurisdiction: conditional on the same proposal, task information, model, and review output, when is the reviewer… ▽ More Multi-agent language-model systems often add a reviewer to improve an upstream agent's decision. Yet a reviewer can both repair errors and replace decisions that were already correct. We study this as a problem of institutional jurisdiction: conditional on the same proposal, task information, model, and review output, when is the reviewer authorized to make its recommendation binding? We compare broad override authority with an evidence gate that permits replacement only after the reviewer produces a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation and a compliant repair . Across two locally run open-weight models, 96 spatial-policy tasks, and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark, the gate sharply reduces corruption of correct proposals while retaining most repairs of violations. The directions of this tradeoff are partly implied by the rule; its magnitude depends on reviewer transitions and upstream proposal states. A prospective validation then gives the reviewer an explicit choice to retain, replace, or escalate. This eliminates correct-proposal corruption for Qwen, but Mistral still replaces all 48 correct proposals; Qwen also declines every welfare-only repair that Mistral frequently attempts. Thus interface design changes reviewer behavior but is not a model-independent safeguard. The result is not that restricted review is universally better. It is that reviewer competence, action interface, and binding jurisdiction jointly determine both the correction domain and the corruption surface. △ Less Submitted 12 September, 2026; originally announced November 2026. Comments: 11 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code, frozen outputs, and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/tofuadmiral/institutional-representation-abm

title: OmniScribble: Mixed-Initiative Authoring of Animated Sketches through Inspectable and Repairable AI Decisions
text: arXiv:2611.04284 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.HC OmniScribble: Mixed-Initiative Authoring of Animated Sketches through Inspectable and Repairable AI Decisions Authors: Hien Trinh , Tan-Hiep To , Trung-Nghia Le Abstract : AI-assisted creative tools reduce the effort of authoring content, but delegating creative decisions to AI can make it difficult for… ▽ More AI-assisted creative tools reduce the effort of authoring content, but delegating creative decisions to AI can make it difficult for authors to understand, correct, or redirect work. We present OmniScribble, a system for animating multi-object sketches that treats object decomposition and motion planning as editable artifacts. Rather than generating animation end-to-end, OmniScribble presents AI proposals at verification checkpoints, where authors can accept, repair , or regenerate them. Both manual and AI-assisted authoring operate on the intermediate representation and rendering pipeline, allowing us to isolate AI delegation. In a within-subject study with eight participants, AI-assisted authoring yielded a median within-participant reduction in completion time of 71.4\%, while perceived control and motion-intent alignment remained high. Interaction traces and interviews show that participants adapted to AI errors by repairing local issues, regenerating mismatches, and accepting proposals. These findings suggest that inspectable, repairable delegation enables generative automation while maintaining control over the outcome. △ Less Submitted 2 November, 2026; originally announced November 2026.

title: Creating Hybrid Interactive Narrative Systems with LLM: From Formal Description to Evaluation
text: arXiv:2611.02807 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.CL cs.HC Creating Hybrid Interactive Narrative Systems with LLM: From Formal Description to Evaluation Authors: Jules Clerc , Domitile Lourdeaux , Mohamed Sallak , Marc Ravaine Abstract : …state-transition representation and evaluated, independently of how the manager works internally, with shared indicators of four properties: player agency, EM controllability, author intent, and robustness. We implement three contrasting managers, based respectively on open generation, Monte Carlo… ▽ More Interactive narratives let users shape a story while an Experience Manager (EM) keeps it coherent, balancing player freedom against authorial control. Large Language Models now enable a new generation of hybrid EMs, which combine run-time generation from free-text input with symbolic narrative control. However, their heterogeneity makes them hard to compare: A manager's behaviour is generally tied to the unique and specific scenario in which it operates, and much of its decision-making takes place outside of any explicit and verifiable structure. We address this with an LLM-based narrative platform whose managers are interchangeable modules operating over a shared symbolic world model of facts, operations, and goals. Because every applied operation carries explicit preconditions and effects, each session can be analysed as a plan through a common state-transition representation and evaluated, independently of how the manager works internally, with shared indicators of four properties: player agency, EM controllability, author intent, and robustness. We implement three contrasting managers, based respectively on open generation, Monte Carlo repair , and autonomous characters, and compare them through functional analysis on an interactive Little Red Riding Hood scenario. The results show that no manager dominates on every property, giving authors and EM designers a concrete basis to select a manager according to their priorities. △ Less Submitted 2 November, 2026; originally announced November 2026. Journal ref: 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026), IEEE Computer Society, Nov 2026, Boca Raton, United States

title: Networked Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web
text: arXiv:2611.02407 [ pdf ] cs.CR cs.AI cs.CY Networked Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web Authors: Bryan C. Boots Abstract : …reports unchanged. We examine these networked consequences of synthetic social engineering (SSE), deliberately misleading influence intended to redirect AI recipients from authorized objectives. Our framework connects social influence, information aggregation, and misinformation correction research to observable evidence and permission boundaries. It separat… ▽ More Several genuine AI services may repeat one unsupported source, and correcting that source may leave later reports unchanged. We examine these networked consequences of synthetic social engineering (SSE), deliberately misleading influence intended to redirect AI recipients from authorized objectives. Our framework connects social influence, information aggregation, and misinformation correction research to observable evidence and permission boundaries. It separates originating attempts from legitimate intermediaries' work and distinguishes identity, evidentiary support, and authorization . We test four relationships using Qwen3-4B and two briefing tasks across 1,080 research units in our Agent Service Exchange and Evidence Commons (ASE-EC). Multiple dependent publishers produced no supported increase in unsupported verification (78.3% versus 75.0%); publication availability left downstream violation reach at 40.0% in both arms. These comparisons direct attention to weaknesses already present in the reference workflows. High reference error rates and retained private handoffs preclude claims of immunity to social pressure. Without scope revalidation, corrections identifying dependent reports reduced residual invalid decisions from 14.4% to 8.1% at equal notification coverage and increased successful report repairs from 16/63 to 36/63. Scope revalidation added no demonstrated protection, and clearing dialogue offered no established recovery advantage. Unapproved requests persisted, all blocked by an external gateway. For designers, the findings caution against treating publisher count as independent evidence, notification as repair , or cleared histories as recovery. They support targeting corrections at reused reports, assessing factual and permission recovery separately, and enforcing authorization at execution. △ Less Submitted 1 November, 2026; originally announced November 2026. ACM Class: K.6.5; I.2.11

title: Trustworthy Execution of Industrial Agents
text: arXiv:2611.02300 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE cs.MA Trustworthy Execution of Industrial Agents Authors: Zhongjie Wang , Mingyi Liu , Xiang He , Xiao Wang , Shuang Yu , Kai Wang Abstract : …We present a framework for trustworthy industrial-agent execution within a single enterprise governance domain. Eight control domains assign responsibilities across authority , planning, composition, tool execution, actual effects, evidence, baseline and use governance, and recovery and evolution. A four-plane architecture and three control chains connect th… ▽ More Industrial agents increasingly modify persistent engineering objects rather than merely generate answers. Authentication and successful calls cannot establish whether intended changes occurred, evidence supports a conclusion, or historical results remain applicable. We present a framework for trustworthy industrial-agent execution within a single enterprise governance domain. Eight control domains assign responsibilities across authority , planning, composition, tool execution, actual effects, evidence, baseline and use governance, and recovery and evolution. A four-plane architecture and three control chains connect these responsibilities through typed objects and version-bound interfaces. The specification separates tool returns from actual engineering effects, evidence coverage from engineering judgment, and historical lifecycle state from current applicability. Multi-agent handoffs are an architectural extension examined through deterministic interface tests. Distinct prototypes examine selected mechanisms using conformance tests, ablations, uncertainty stress, CAD/CAE execution, and local persistence. An OpenFOAM fixture produces COMPLETE coverage with FAIL judgment; an expired-job case requires readmission despite completed computation. CAD and recovery counterexamples expose omitted mandatory checks, discarded negative facts, and inconsistent producer-consumer mappings. Targeted repairs support local regression conclusions. The reported 0/29 hazardous commits measure closed-set specification conformance, not a safety probability. We distinguish the complete framework, implemented paths, and empirical evidence, identifying check-inventory completeness and cross-module fact preservation as prerequisites for extending these results. △ Less Submitted 1 November, 2026; originally announced November 2026. Comments: 80 pages, 16 figures, 37 tables ACM Class: I.2.11; D.2.11; D.2.4

title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning
text: arXiv:2611.01070 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.LG Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning Authors: Dongxu Li Abstract : …consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-R… ▽ More We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes , executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization. △ Less Submitted 31 October, 2026; originally announced November 2026.

title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results
text: arXiv:2610.42066 [ pdf ] cs.AI cs.CL The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results Authors: Omer Asim Ozturk , Cihan Aydiner Abstract : …each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate pr… ▽ More AI answers require more than apparent correctness: reviewers need to inspect their recorded basis. We introduce the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation. We reference KLM v0.3 (repository tag v0.3.0). Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author -reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work. △ Less Submitted 30 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 47 pages, 1 figure, 14 tables. Includes Appendix A

title: Reparo: Synthesizing and Validating Access Control Policies
text: arXiv:2610.41800 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE cs.CR Reparo: Synthesizing and Validating Access Control Policies Authors: Ayesha Binte Mostofa , Gehao Zhang , Sam Stern , Juan Zhai , Pubali Datta Abstract : Writing correct access control policies for software applications is difficult because it requires expertise in the authorization language and a thorough understanding of the application's… ▽ More Writing correct access control policies for software applications is difficult because it requires expertise in the authorization language and a thorough understanding of the application's authorization requirements. Existing synthesis and mining approaches assume explicit authorization inputs and a trusted reference policy. However, authorization logic is often distributed across code, comments, and documentation rather than captured in a single artifact, and developer-defined policies in real-world application repositories are often incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. We present Reparo, an LLM-aided pipeline for access control policy synthesis, repair , and validation. Reparo collects repository evidence for authorization intent and uses it to guide an LLM in generating an initial policy. It then uses official policy-language validation tools to identify and automatically repair errors. For semantic validation, a different LLM derives a behavioral oracle from the same repository evidence, consisting of concrete authorization requests with expected allow or deny decisions, which Reparo executes against the generated policy. We manually assess the oracle on a statistically sized sample of 390 test cases. We evaluate Reparo on 228 real-world GitHub repositories that use Cedar, OpenFGA, or Rego. In these repositories, 40.6-55.7% of the repository policies fail their language's validation tool, whereas Reparo produces 99.0-100% valid policies after repair . Agreement with the oracle is 98.2-99.6% for OpenFGA, 82.0-86.5% for Cedar, and 76.3-80.2% for Rego. Manual review confirms 91.5-96.9% of the sampled test cases as correct. Synthesizing and validating the policy for one repository takes about five minutes and costs $0.55-$1.57. These results show that repository evidence can support both access policy synthesis and independent validation, even when no reliable reference policy exists. △ Less Submitted 30 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 22 pages, 9 figures

title: DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation
text: arXiv:2610.40754 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.CV DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation Authors: Jeff Tan , Hang Dai , Zeqian Long , Yanzhe Lyu , R. Kenny Jones , Shangzhe Wu , Chen Geng , Jiajun Wu Abstract : …they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on… ▽ More While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user's prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters. △ Less Submitted 29 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: Project page: https://dy-craft.github.io/

title: Omission-Safe Conditional Contracts for Evidence-Closed CI Qualification
text: arXiv:2610.39241 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE Omission-Safe Conditional Contracts for Evidence-Closed CI Qualification Authors: Zhiheng Zhang Abstract : …binding universe, with sound obligations and applicability judgments that preserve established truth under information extension, withdrawing observation facts cannot create authorization . The implementation handles static matrices, dependency guards and bounded pinned reusable workflows, preserving unknown applicability and separating tolerated outcomes fro… ▽ More Continuous-integration evidence is conditional: a workflow determines which jobs should run, while an archive records which jobs remain observable. Reconstructing requirements from those observations lets an omission erase its own obligation. We present a qualification method that compiles a pinned workflow into conditional job requirements independently of target presence, retains a fixed capture inventory, and checks source-complete derivation certificates with a separate implementation. For a fixed source, context, scope and binding universe, with sound obligations and applicability judgments that preserve established truth under information extension, withdrawing observation facts cannot create authorization . The implementation handles static matrices, dependency guards and bounded pinned reusable workflows, preserving unknown applicability and separating tolerated outcomes from evidence coverage. Both implementations match the 45 hand-specified authorization controls, reject 180 source-certificate attacks, and exhibit no authorization gain over 704 distinct proper development erasures. An explicitly witnessed 12-job platform run qualifies in both implementations; all 4,095 proper payload-subset erasures block authorization . A frozen collection spans 240 runs in eight workflow families across six projects. All 160 evaluation source certificates independently validate, but unavailable historical execution-source identities leave actual qualification open. Initial gate diagnoses agree on 155/160 runs; a preserved unknown-propagation repair yields 160/160 agreement in a retrospective rerun. The study establishes bounded source extraction and omission resistance, rather than natural-fault prevalence or producer authenticity. △ Less Submitted 28 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 11 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables

title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
text:
arXiv:2610.37786 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments Authors: Tianci Xie , Zikun Cai , Chaoyun Zhang , Pinxue Guo , Bingxuan Li , Rui Zheng , Hang Yan Abstract : …We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and… ▽ More Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities.
  We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization . An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture.
  We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything △ Less Submitted 27 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 25 pages, 6 figures

title: A Counterexample to KL1 Completeness and a Complete Disjunctive Calculus
text: arXiv:2610.37107 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.LO A Counterexample to KL1 Completeness and a Complete Disjunctive Calculus Authors: Damiano Presa , Fabio Aurelio D'Asaro , Massimiliano Badino Abstract : …over acts. Its consequence relation is operational: a rule follows from a set of rules when adjoining it leaves the set of outcomes unchanged for every input. The authors proved their calculus sound and conjectured that it is complete. We show that the conjecture fails: for distinct atoms $b,c,d$ the rules $\top \diamond\to b \lor d$, $b \diamond\to c$,… ▽ More The logic KL$_1$ of Evans, Sergot and Stephenson formalizes Kant's rules as conditional imperatives $B \square\to C$ and permissives $B \diamond\to C$ over acts. Its consequence relation is operational: a rule follows from a set of rules when adjoining it leaves the set of outcomes unchanged for every input. The authors proved their calculus sound and conjectured that it is complete. We show that the conjecture fails: for distinct atoms $b,c,d$ the rules $\top \diamond\to b \lor d$, $b \diamond\to c$, $d \diamond\to c$ and $c \square\to b \lor d$ entail $\top \diamond\to c$, which is not derivable. Non-derivability is proved by an invariant that holds at every derivation depth and for arbitrary intermediate atoms. The obstruction is the side condition of may-trans, which requires each new act to bring with it a single intermediary act. Replacing it by a disjunctive side condition yields may-trans-disj, a strict generalization from which the original rule is derivable. Using a local characterization of entailment, we prove the repaired calculus sound for arbitrary sets of rules and complete for finite ones, and we show that, with finite inputs, completeness cannot be extended to infinite sets. The main results on KL$_1$ are formalized in Agda. For KL$_2$ we observe that the published reduction to KL$_1$ passes through infinite rule sets; re-establishing the decomposition for finite rule sets, we prove that KL$_2$ with the disjunctive rule is sound and complete for finite sets of rules. We close with remarks on KL$_3$ and on the significance of completeness for the relation between the operational and the inferential questions of Kant's logic. △ Less Submitted 27 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: CodeMeepo: A Multi-Agent Workflow for Repository-Level Code Migration and Optimization
text:
arXiv:2610.34633 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE cs.AI CodeMeepo: A Multi-Agent Workflow for Repository-Level Code Migration and Optimization Authors: Farzad Habibi , Changrong Wu , Jinzhou Jiang , Guohan Lu Abstract : …a multi-agent pipeline for complete and efficient migration of large repositories. Each milestone is evaluated against a fixed external oracle that the agents neither author nor modify. A separate parity assessment compares source and target components in scope and adds identified gaps back into the plan as required work. Ordered milestones limit the scope… ▽ More Repository-level code migration rewrites an entire project in a new programming language while preserving its observable behavior. It is challenging because behavior spans interdependent modules, dependencies and build infrastructure must be adapted to the target ecosystem, and the source code is often the only specification.
  Large language model agents can now attempt these migrations end to end, but three challenges remain. First, an agent that writes both the translation and its acceptance tests may overlook the same requirements in both, leaving missing or incorrect behavior undetected. Second, large repositories can exceed a model's context window, and dividing the work into smaller tasks does not ensure that all required behavior is migrated. Third, even behaviorally correct translations may be slower than the original implementation.
  We present CodeMeepo, a multi-agent pipeline for complete and efficient migration of large repositories. Each milestone is evaluated against a fixed external oracle that the agents neither author nor modify. A separate parity assessment compares source and target components in scope and adds identified gaps back into the plan as required work. Ordered milestones limit the scope of each task, while cumulative regression checks guard against breaking already-migrated behavior. A benchmark-guided optimization phase addresses performance, followed by full-suite conformance testing and repair . Eight specialized agent roles communicate through file artifacts, and a deterministic state machine governs repair , deferral, scope changes, and termination.
  On nine subjects in three language pairs, CodeMeepo achieves the best pass rate on every subject and passes 18% more tests than a state-of-the-art multi-agent baseline using the same model. On a production daemon, its optimization phase improves half of the benchmarks, by 25% on average. △ Less Submitted 25 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: OneCodeReviewBench: Typed Decisions for Code Review and Search
text: arXiv:2610.33389 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE OneCodeReviewBench: Typed Decisions for Code Review and Search Authors: Mohamad Mohebifar , Alex Bit Abstract : …categorical, and ordered answers. Explicit contracts specify runtime assumptions, source scope, and answer criteria; separate evidence records support reference review. One author reviewed 150 cases; two additional engineers reviewed 100 of those cases. We compare ten model--adapter systems on the same cases and contracts: OpenAI Decisions reaches 81.3% Boo… ▽ More Code review requires finding functional bugs, memory-safety errors, security weaknesses, and performance problems across languages and software stacks. Tools can express bounded parts of this work as decisions about supplied code. We present OneCodeReviewBench, 1,968 synthetic cases across 12 programming languages and YAML, with Boolean, categorical, and ordered answers. Explicit contracts specify runtime assumptions, source scope, and answer criteria; separate evidence records support reference review. One author reviewed 150 cases; two additional engineers reviewed 100 of those cases. We compare ten model--adapter systems on the same cases and contracts: OpenAI Decisions reaches 81.3% Boolean balanced accuracy; Kev-27B reaches 76.8% Choice accuracy and Score mean absolute error of 0.367. Excluding two families with incomplete contracts preserves these leaders. Additional comparisons cover 586 cases with raw symbol search and 40 with a bounded Python import resolver; the resolver matches all 40 references within its supported profile. A versioned artifact reproduces these analyses and retains the 85 cases with matching engineer answers; the reported review subset excludes two incomplete-contract cases. Remaining reviewer disagreements and repaired inputs require resolution; repository-scale transfer and matched latency/cost evaluation remain future work. △ Less Submitted 23 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 6 pages, 6 tables. Dataset and reproduction artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23604731

title: Runtime BiDi Structural Verification Catches Right-to-Left Layout Defects that Accessibility, Actionability, and Logical-Property Linting Miss
text: arXiv:2610.32934 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE cs.HC Runtime BiDi Structural Verification Catches Right-to-Left Layout Defects that Accessibility, Actionability, and Logical-Property Linting Miss Authors: Karan Yadav Abstract : Bidirectional (right-to-left, RTL) layout defects arise when interfaces authored with physical directional CSS (margin-left, border-left, text-align:left) are rendered under dir="rtl" without being mirrored. Accessibility engines (axe-core), actionability engines (Playwright), and even Stylelint's current core logical-property rule fail to locali… ▽ More Bidirectional (right-to-left, RTL) layout defects arise when interfaces authored with physical directional CSS (margin-left, border-left, text-align:left) are rendered under dir="rtl" without being mirrored. Accessibility engines (axe-core), actionability engines (Playwright), and even Stylelint's current core logical-property rule fail to localise these defects. We present runtime structural invariants -- a zero-golden mode over computed style and geometry, and a bidi-conservative differential mode -- that catch them in a headless browser. On a held-out benchmark of 14 real RTL bugs reconstructed from dated fix commits in Bootstrap and Material Components Web, the detector recovers 13/14 (2 via zero-golden, 11 via the differential mode), with no false alarm on any patched version; on the actual committed historical bootstrap.rtl.css it catches 1 of 2 attempted. It reports 0 false positives on 16 negative LTR-island cases and, in both modes, on 43 unmodified real components across four design systems and three RTL architectures (rule-of-three 95% upper bound <= 7%), and it surfaced a real directional defect in the current Bulma 1.0.4. By contrast, Stylelint's core rule emits an identical 1744 warnings on Bootstrap's LTR and correct-RTL builds, pseudo-localisation detects none of the mirroring bugs, and a naive pixel mirror-and-diff reaches only F1 0.87 with a test-set-tuned threshold. The two modes are complementary: zero-golden is the sole detector of the decoration/styling-asymmetry class (5/6) but false-flags the correct logical border-inline-end, while the differential detects none of that class yet never false-alarms and is empirically exact on the block-level inset/margin class. We scope this paper to detection; repair is future work. △ Less Submitted 23 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 7 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables

title: PaperFormalizer: Author -in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
text: arXiv:2610.31810 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.LO PaperFormalizer: Author -in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean Authors: Jiyuan Tan , Jose Blanchet , Vasilis Syrgkanis Abstract : Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency gra… ▽ More Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair , in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org. △ Less Submitted 26 October, 2026; v1 submitted 22 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling
text:
arXiv:2610.30184 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.CR cs.AI cs.SE Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling Authors: Rui Melo , Andre Duarte , Aditya Oke , Shubham Gandhi , Nachiket Kotalwar , Rui Abreu , Lei Li , Carolyn Rose Abstract : …queries that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a manually authored process into an iterative process of automated discovery and repair . ▽ More Security bugs often slip past static analysis not because they are impossible to detect, but because detection rules have not yet been written for the code in front of us. New frameworks, APIs, and coding idioms continually create such gaps, leaving developers to discover failures and manually encode new rules. We present SESAA, a framework in which an Large Language Model (LLM) agent starts from no rules and iteratively evolves a set of readable and auditable joern queries.
  The agent receives feedback only from a second LLM critic, which inspects flagged and unflagged code to identify likely false alarms and suspected misses, without access to ground-truth labels. The agent then uses this feedback to revise its queries. On the OWASP Benchmark for Python, SESAA reaches a mean F1 of 0.742 across 8 independent runs, well above the default configurations of five widely used tools and comparable to the strongest of them once it is tuned with access to ground-truth labels that SESAA never sees. In a pilot on real-world Python projects, queries induced from code available before a vulnerability was introduced detect 10 of 19 subsequent CVEs, including 9 detected by rules written for the same repository.
  The resulting detector is a set of executable, human-readable queries that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a manually authored process into an iterative process of automated discovery and repair . △ Less Submitted 20 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: Cryptanalysis and Repair of "Decentralized Multi- authority ABE for NC$^1$ from BDH"
text: arXiv:2610.29224 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.CR Cryptanalysis and Repair of "Decentralized Multi- authority ABE for NC$^1$ from BDH" Authors: Xingwang Wang Abstract : …variant of Datta, Komargodski, and Waters (Journal of Cryptology, 2023). The attack succeeds with probability one in the claimed static security model using one corrupt authority and two users, each unauthorized even when granted the corrupt… ▽ More We present a plaintext-recovery attack on both the DBDH-based construction and the CBDH-based variant of Datta, Komargodski, and Waters (Journal of Cryptology, 2023). The attack succeeds with probability one in the claimed static security model using one corrupt authority and two users, each unauthorized even when granted the corrupt authority's attribute. The flaw is an invalid extension of the LSSS matrix-normalization lemma originating with Rouselakis and Waters (FC,~2015): preserving complete-share distributions does not preserve coordinate-wise ciphertext masks, which a corrupt authority can expose to remove identity binding from other users' shares. For both variants, replacing these masks with independent full linear sharings of zero preserves correctness and restores ciphertext-distribution invariance. We prove static security of both repaired variants in the random oracle model under their respective BDH assumptions, using the original hardcore-bit convention for the CBDH variant. Both proofs allow adaptive identity-hash queries. The modification retains the original matrix-width and row-labeling restrictions, keys, decryption, and ciphertext size, requiring only additional encryption randomness and finite-field arithmetic. We also attack both multi- authority attribute-based inner-product functional encryption constructions of Datta and Pal (PKC, 2023) and establish correctness and matrix-substitution invariance of the same repair . We prove static security of the repaired small-universe construction under asymmetric DBDH. For the large-universe construction, we identify a missing source-group encoding in the original reduction and give a complete static security proof under an augmented $L$-DBDH assumption, whose generic bilinear group hardness we establish. △ Less Submitted 26 October, 2026; v1 submitted 21 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
text: arXiv:2610.29014 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.GR cs.HC GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development Authors: William Huang , David Li , Xiang 'Anthony' Chen , Xun Qian , Nels Numan , Zhongyi Zhou , Hyunsung Cho , Salman Muin Kayser Chishti , Ding Xia , Xincheng Huang , Jiahao Ren , Faraz Faruqi , Tianyu Xu , Yang Zhang , David Kim , Ruofei Du Abstract : Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends… ▽ More Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert- authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs , and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing. △ Less Submitted 22 October, 2026; v1 submitted 20 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 37 pages, 10 figures. Code available at https://github.com/whuang37/genxr-bench

title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement
text:
arXiv:2610.27465 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.CL cs.SE Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement Authors: De Wang , Peng Qi Abstract : …starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author . How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $σ$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM j… ▽ More Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author . How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $σ$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM judge -- agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off.
  Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform's own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the $τ^2$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform's LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17 percent of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs . Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier's strength has been measured. △ Less Submitted 19 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AgenticOS. 6 pages + appendix

title: Compile Once, Run Cheap: Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents, and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds
text: arXiv:2610.25114 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.RO cs.AI cs.LG Compile Once, Run Cheap: Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents, and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds Authors: Jingwen Bai , Guochao Bai , Canbo Zhang , Shuangqi Li , Minchao Hu , Weichun Huang , Shuang Liu Abstract : …so new manipulation capability costs demonstrations per task or a frontier model in every episode. We study a third route: a strong general model acts only as an offline author that writes, runs, diagnoses and… ▽ More Embodied AI lacks the data-rich pretraining that gave language models their agents and skills, so new manipulation capability costs demonstrations per task or a frontier model in every episode. We study a third route: a strong general model acts only as an offline author that writes, runs, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in simulation until it passes an exam on layouts drawn after freezing; the frozen skill then runs as code alone or under a cheap caller that reads only its description. We call this skill-level recursive self-improvement Skill-RSI and specify a compile protocol (isolated, audited author ; hidden validation layouts; no-feedback and inherit-only controls; tamper-evident ledger) and a reuse protocol that runs the identical files with executors from another model family. On 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with cluttered tables, Claude Code compiled 4 tasks into 7 frozen skills, 5 from a first draft needing only qualification, at USD 4.29-8.22 of author cost each (USD 55 per skill counting the 13 failed campaigns). The other three tasks did not compile in 18 campaigns, including five with GPT-6 and a pre-registered 150-layout run: on the hardest task every campaign scored 78-95 of 100 but had 3-16 safety aborts, failing the gate of 95% success with zero aborts; a 100-episode exam bounds an abort rate only to 3.6%. On hidden layouts, repair that inherits the previous version beat from-scratch rewriting in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns (sign test p = 0.004); an inherit-only lineage attributes most of the gap to inheritance, with development feedback adding a little (3 of 3, p = 0.125). Write-once campaigns found no detectable first-draft effect of practice (minimum detectable effect 14 points). The frozen skills kept 148/150 successes on new layouts with no model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller at USD 0.00028-0.00054 per episode; no direct-control baseline was run. △ Less Submitted 18 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 28 pages, 4 figures, 13 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Orillusion/embodied-skill-rsi

title: VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research
text: arXiv:2610.24329 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.SE cs.AI VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research Authors: Minbo Ma , Honglin Zhang , Bangtao Zhou , Chunguang Yu , Dasheng Ju , Yichen Shen , Fengli Xu , Yong Li Abstract : …coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self- authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the gene… ▽ More Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self- authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the generated program and its checks share omissions or misinterpretations of task requirements, alongside incomplete verification coverage and ineffective optimization strategies. We propose VERAS, a verification-guided adaptive search harness for reliable OR that uses verification evidence to prioritize feasibility repair , constraint-coverage review, and solution-quality improvement. VERAS combines task-specific solution checkers with a separate verification agent to examine candidate solutions against the task requirements. It uses verification feedback to guide feasibility repair , additional constraint checking, and objective improvement, while candidate acceptance criteria screen revisions for deterioration in output validity or constraint satisfaction. On ORAgentBench, VERAS achieves a 42.99% pass rate, exceeding the reported 35.51% of Codex using the same LLM. Across two industrial-scale OR problems, VERAS reduces inter-datacenter peak bandwidth by 10.34% relative to native Codex and lowers annualized distribution network planning costs by 6.28% compared with expert-designed solutions. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/holimario/VERAS. △ Less Submitted 16 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: Monitor-Validity Failures: LLM Safety Evidence Paths at Evolving Framework Boundaries
text: arXiv:2610.23362 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.CR cs.SE Monitor-Validity Failures: LLM Safety Evidence Paths at Evolving Framework Boundaries Authors: Junchi Liao Abstract : …result before the block decision. This differs from jailbreaks and detector errors because the evidence is already recognized yet disconnected from enforcement. We study this repair -boundary signature with canary contracts: parent/fixed confirmation units that place a known payload only on the changed evidence surface and record monitor visibility together w… ▽ More Modern LLM applications rely on runtime monitors that inspect tool calls, traces, streams, detector outputs, and verifier inputs. This creates an interface-reliability problem: a framework path may remain operational while policy-relevant evidence never reaches its decision point. In one representative case, a regex detector returned a positive match, but the framework stranded the result before the block decision. This differs from jailbreaks and detector errors because the evidence is already recognized yet disconnected from enforcement. We study this repair -boundary signature with canary contracts: parent/fixed confirmation units that place a known payload only on the changed evidence surface and record monitor visibility together with the downstream decision for action-boundary cases. Applying the protocol to public framework repairs , we confirm 18 evidence-path failures across 11 LLM or agent safety project groups and four implementation ecosystems. Nine are established-boundary repairs , eight are new-surface policy-coverage gaps, and one is a boundary-only evidence case. Fourteen reach E1 enforcement boundaries: seven native action outcomes, six configured enforcement boundaries, and one synthetic-consumer consequence. The remaining cases affect verifier, safety-prompt, or observability channels. The cases form carrier, adapter, authority , and surface families and show how ordinary application behavior can remain intact while a safety-specific evidence path misses its decision. Exact revisions, deterministic outcomes, negative controls, and a frozen prospective audit document the confirmation rule. Monitor assumptions therefore need regression tests at the schemas, streams, tools, and adapters that frameworks evolve. △ Less Submitted 16 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: Author -in-the-loop Agentic Reproducibility Auditing for a Machine Learning Conference
text: arXiv:2610.22465 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.HC Author -in-the-loop Agentic Reproducibility Auditing for a Machine Learning Conference Authors: Yukun Dong , Linjun Zhang , Tian Zheng Abstract : Reproducibility checks during peer review require a shared understanding of what authors ' code is expected to reproduce. We present an… ▽ More Reproducibility checks during peer review require a shared understanding of what authors ' code is expected to reproduce. We present an author -in-the-loop collaborative audit that makes author declarations explicit inputs to an AI agent's investigation and assessment. A structured checklist records reproduction instructions and limitations; a two-stage workflow on GitHub connects agent checks to author clarification, revision, and agent reassessment. The agent separately assesses whether results have been reproduced and whether authors need to provide clarification or make repairs , while human reviewers approve requests and decide whether concerns are resolved. We deployed the system across 36 conference papers and 133 experimental tables and figures, raising 20 issues after human review. Further checks supported closing all the issues, although full reproduction remained unverified in some cases. We further compared repeated audits with complete and blank checklists to examine how author declarations shaped the agent's investigation and assessment. Our work contributes a collaborative workflow and agent design that use author knowledge to guide reproducibility auditing. The conference deployment provides empirical evidence that this approach can help identify and address reproducibility problems through collaboration among authors , agents, and reviewers. △ Less Submitted 15 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 23 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables

title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents
text: arXiv:2610.21463 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.CL cs.AI cs.LG Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents Authors: Zilin Wang , Yinhong Liu , Chao Chen , Qun Liu , Zhijiang Guo Abstract : …model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, an… ▽ More Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On $τ^2$-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic. △ Less Submitted 15 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: Learning When to Withdraw: Curriculum Coverage and Rule-Specific Failures in Fine-Tuned Language Agents
text: arXiv:2610.21045 [ pdf ] cs.AI Learning When to Withdraw: Curriculum Coverage and Rule-Specific Failures in Fine-Tuned Language Agents Authors: Mohamed Abouzahra Abstract : Tool-using language agents must revise prepared actions when evidence changes or authority is revoked. Selective withdrawal means suspending affected actions, preserving supported work, and resuming only after sufficient… ▽ More Tool-using language agents must revise prepared actions when evidence changes or authority is revoked. Selective withdrawal means suspending affected actions, preserving supported work, and resuming only after sufficient repair . We study supervised fine-tuning in NAQD-Env, a synthetic environment with explicit dependencies and a deterministic reference policy. Four LoRA checkpoints of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct compare an original curriculum with an enriched one, the latter under three system-prompt framings with identical views and targets. Three instruction-tuned baselines and all four checkpoints are evaluated under three inference prompts on fresh validation cases, held-out dependency families, and held-out structural combinations. Under the naqd prompt, SFT checkpoints reach decision agreement of 0.77-0.92 and withdrawal recall of 0.46-0.86, versus 0.45-0.63 and at most 0.06 for the baselines. Rule-level diagnostics qualify these gains. The original-curriculum checkpoint wrongly withdraws 26 of 34 actions with surviving alternative support; enriched checkpoints withdraw 0-1. Conversely, all SFT checkpoints narrow prohibited combinations less often than the 7B and 8B baselines, a case absent from both curricula. Delegation results show more withdrawal but poorer preservation of independently authorized actions, and all four checkpoints omit valid event reports. Framing contrasts vary across metrics and splits and do not establish a reproducible advantage or equivalence. One training run per arm, jointly changed curriculum properties, prior evaluation exposure, and baseline-SFT quantization differences limit causal attribution. The contribution is a method for detecting rule-specific regressions that aggregate accuracy can conceal, not evidence that fine-tuning alone ensures agent safety. △ Less Submitted 14 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: Compiling Expert Procedures into Verified Programs: When a Small Model Is Enough
text: arXiv:2610.19148 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.SC Compiling Expert Procedures into Verified Programs: When a Small Model Is Enough Authors: Vishvesh Bhat , Asad Aali , Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin Abstract : …including an 8B model. The construction, PLVR , takes the reasoning traces of a teacher, Kimi-K3, clusters their segments to locate recurring operations, has a frontier model author one typed primitive per operation, each run by a small frozen model and assembles the program by A* search over a mined rule library, under a reference-action objective. At infe… ▽ More In procedural tool-use domains, how much of the gap between base models is procedure rather than capability? We build an explicit program from a teacher's traces and run it in front of unchanged small models, including an 8B model. The construction, PLVR , takes the reasoning traces of a teacher, Kimi-K3, clusters their segments to locate recurring operations, has a frontier model author one typed primitive per operation, each run by a small frozen model and assembles the program by A* search over a mined rule library, under a reference-action objective. At inference the program takes one of two forms: for troubleshooting and tool search it produces the chain of thought the student would otherwise generate for itself, and the student acts on it; for multi-turn tool matching the student proposes each action and the program checks, repairs , or retries it before it goes out. On the official tau2-Bench Retail and Telecom test sets and on LiveMCPBench, with three Nemotron base models and the same program for each, the answer depends on the domain. On Telecom, Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2% under the program, and every Nemotron student reaches 93.3-94.4%, against at most 58.2% for fine-tuning on the same traces, prompt optimisation of the student, or two token-matched baselines. With Granite-4.2-8B as the student, the program is within 2 to 3 points of the Nemotron students on Telecom and within 3 on Retail, and 3 to 13 points below them on LiveMCPBench: where the domain is procedural an 8B student is enough, and on tool search the student still matters. On Retail and LiveMCPBench the program is competitive with the best baseline. The spread between base models shrinks from about 7 points to about 2, averaged over the suites, with no weights changed. △ Less Submitted 16 October, 2026; v1 submitted 13 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: AssetForge: Asset-Augmented Task Synthesis for Business Automation Agents
text: arXiv:2610.18330 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI AssetForge: Asset-Augmented Task Synthesis for Business Automation Agents Authors: Xiangrui Liu , Shuo Tang , Siheng Chen Abstract : …business automation agents requires executable tasks that connect a natural-language request to an application state and a verifiable end state. Traditional Rubrics requires Authors to recreate application interfaces, initial records, policy evidence, and outcome checks for each task, entangling business logic with repeated infrastructure work. We introduce… ▽ More Training business automation agents requires executable tasks that connect a natural-language request to an application state and a verifiable end state. Traditional Rubrics requires Authors to recreate application interfaces, initial records, policy evidence, and outcome checks for each task, entangling business logic with repeated infrastructure work. We introduce AssetForge, an asset-augmented task-construction pipeline that pairs a reusable construction-asset library with task-specific Rubrics. The assets provide application interfaces, world-state components, policy/evidence carriers, and native assertion definitions; the Rubric directs their instantiation for a particular business task. Executable checks and an additional model-based review validate each candidate, return targeted feedback, and support bounded repair before acceptance. On AutomationBench v1.0.6 public-600, fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 6,000 AssetForge examples yields 41.17% on the official strict pass@1 metric, 4.4 times the 9.33% base score (+31.83 points). With the same backbone and GLM-5.3 supervision, AssetForge reaches 41.17% versus 30.33% for traditional Rubrics, a 10.84-point gain (35.7% relative) at the same accepted-example scale (6,000 versus 6,000 examples). Both DeepSeek- and GLM-supervised AssetForge models improve AppWorld completion over the base model on Test-Normal and Test-Challenge. These results establish the advantage of AssetForge's complete construction pipeline on AutomationBench public: the coupled asset-Rubric interface directs Authors toward business logic, while executable checks and model-based review validate their tasks. △ Less Submitted 21 October, 2026; v1 submitted 13 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026. Comments: 22 pages, 5 figures

title: Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization
text: arXiv:2610.16838 [ pdf , ps , other ] cs.AI cs.SE Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization Authors: Huihao Jing , Shaojin Chen , Wenbin Hu , Yuxuan Liu , Haochen Shi , Zhongwei Xie , Haoran Li , Yangqiu Song Abstract : As language-model agents write code, move money and change records on behalf of users, deciding whether an action is authorized has become a central safety problem. Guardrails are often placed in front of these actions, yet few evaluations ask whether their decisions follow… ▽ More As language-model agents write code, move money and change records on behalf of users, deciding whether an action is authorized has become a central safety problem. Guardrails are often placed in front of these actions, yet few evaluations ask whether their decisions follow authorization : blocking unauthorized actions while still allowing the same actions under valid permission. We introduce \bench{}, a benchmark that contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation in its language track. It combines expert-annotated natural-language scenarios with executed and verified operations, plus externally sourced native-policy requests. \bench{} checks each decision for correctness, usability and resulting effect, and tracks each request across guardrail changes. Our experiments show that many blocked operations stem from failed reviews, not correct denials. Repairing the output format restores usable decisions but changes which authorized requests are honored, and adding a second reviewer removes some errors while rejecting valid authorization . Guardrails should therefore be evaluated on both the unauthorized actions they stop and the authorized actions they let through. △ Less Submitted 12 October, 2026; originally announced October 2026.

title: From Product Evidence to Access Rights: Auditing and Routing Non-Firm Grid Connections
text: arXiv:2610.15510 [ pdf , ps , other ] math.OC From Product Evidence to Access Rights: Auditing and Routing Non-Firm Grid Connections Authors: Alban Kryeziu , Stuart X. Zhu , Evrim Ursavas Abstract : …and fixes directional restriction calendars from public residual-load and day-ahead price-timing signals. Stage B audits the submitted calendar and one bounded common repair , tests joint threshold attainability under the shared annual budget, and applies an aggregation-aware Power Transfer Distribution Factor (PTDF) certificate. Stage C treats the resulting… ▽ More Non-firm connection products can accelerate grid access while reinforcements are delayed, but their planning value depends on evidence supporting the contractual promise. We develop a one-way evidence-to-access framework for calendarized products. Stage A constructs and fixes directional restriction calendars from public residual-load and day-ahead price-timing signals. Stage B audits the submitted calendar and one bounded common repair , tests joint threshold attainability under the shared annual budget, and applies an aggregation-aware Power Transfer Distribution Factor (PTDF) certificate. Stage C treats the resulting ledger as fixed in queue-aware allocation and intervention planning. In the primary policy-package evaluation, the evidence-supported menu returns the same $2.119$~GW allocation as firm-only access, whereas authorizing the uniformly derated fallback raises awards to $6.442$~GW and reduces backlog from $136.076$ to $113.601$~GW-years; all $4.489$~GW of non-firm awards use the fallback. In a target-free matched control, evidence-routed and state-blind fallback menus attain primary objectives equivalent within EUR~1 and return the same accepted applicants, award years, routes, and intervention portfolio.
